We can use the laws of exponents and the algebra of limits to rewrite the given limit, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{(-3x+1)} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{-3x}\cdot {e}^{1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{-3x}\cdot e \\  & =e\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{-3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the graph of $y={e}^{-3x}:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13943873/assets/c3d9e0bfa0b7514713c01289fc63fde7b0bd0dab525ad50617a9e908fd117060.png)

From the graph, we see that the function decreases to zero as $x$ increases. Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{-3x}=0.
$$

Therefore:

$$
e\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{-3x}=e\cdot 0=0
$$
